synopsis: FCW warns car and truck drivers of an imminent crash ahead but leaves braking to them; the booklet uses this on-road research as a counterpart to the manufacturer's existing proximity warning, not as direct evidence about off-road operators [f11678, f11679, f11686]. Regulatory precedents are likewise on-road: FMVSS No. 127 requires FCW alongside AEB for light vehicles up to 4,536 kg GVWR and does not apply to off-road machines, while NHTSA's heavy-vehicle research and 2023 proposal concern road trucks and buses [f2831, f2535, f1816]. On-road FCW plus AEB reduced rear-end striking crashes by 50% in Cicchino's 2017 study, but insurance evidence also showed a 20% increase in being struck from behind, making automatic stopping a potential trade-off rather than an unqualified benefit [f3459, f3409, f14017]. False-alarm evidence is mixed: an 18% rate was associated with drivers ignoring warnings (12%) or abandoning FCW (11%), whereas simulator warnings with 20–33% false alarms still shortened brake reactions, and a 2025 study found no cry-wolf effect at 33% despite unnecessary braking [f11680, f11681, f11682]. Real-driving false alerts varied from 12% when turning to 2% during lane-keeping, drivers reduced sensitivity over time, and alarms with visible causes harmed trust less; no accepted off-road false-alarm rate was found [f11683, f11684, f11685, f11687]. Validation therefore needs to distinguish measured warning performance from modeled benefit: open-loop replay can establish detection, false-alarm rates and warning timing only for recorded configurations and situations, while a virtual cyclist-overtaking FCW assessment estimated 53–96% fatality reductions depending predominantly on its driver-response model [f5234, f3497].
